p.x:
My favourite place in Thailand is a small island in the south. Every year, my family takes a trip there. We go to see the beautiful beaches and the clear blue sea.
When I was a child, there were not many visitors. Now, many tourists come from all over the world. There are new hotels and restaurants, and some people ride jet skis.
Last year, the island made a new rule: plastic bags are banned. There's a big sign at the port that says, "Please keep our island clean." I think it's a good idea, because I want the island to stay beautiful.

Tourism is very important for Thailand's economy. It provides employment for millions of people, from hotel workers to taxi drivers and tour guides. When tourists stay in a homestay in a village, residents can earn extra money, and local shops benefit too.
However, too many visitors can cause problems. On some islands, cruise ships bring thousands of people at once. Beaches become crowded, and wildlife is disturbed. In some places, there is so much rubbish that the government has had to restrict the number of visitors.
One famous example is Maya Bay in Krabi. After the film 'The Beach', it became extremely popular, and boats and swimmers damaged the coral. In 2018, the bay was closed so that nature could recover. Now there is an entrance fee, and swimming is not allowed. Visitors can also come in the off-season, when there are fewer crowds. Many experts say this kind of planning is necessary to protect Thailand's most beautiful places for the future.

Few industries have grown as dramatically as tourism. Before the pandemic, international arrivals had reached around 1.5 billion a year, and cheap flights and social media continue to send ever larger crowds to the same famous sites. The term 'overtourism' now describes destinations where the number of visitors exceeds a place's carrying capacity, damaging both the environment and residents' quality of life.
The consequences take many forms. In cities such as Venice and Barcelona, the spread of short-term rentals has pushed up housing costs, leading to the displacement of long-term residents. Traditional festivals may become commercialised, performed for cameras rather than for the community. In fragile natural areas, an influx of visitors can destroy what attracted them in the first place: pristine beaches are polluted and reefs lose their colour. Mass tourism also brings an economic paradox known as leakage: when international hotel chains and tour companies dominate, much of the money spent by tourists flows abroad rather than staying in the local economy.
Governments are experimenting with solutions. Some have introduced a daily quota or require visitors to obtain a permit; others charge a tourist levy to fund conservation. Higher prices may deter some travellers, but supporters argue that fewer, higher-spending visitors are better than vast numbers of day-trippers. Areas that have closed temporarily have shown that nature can regenerate surprisingly quickly.
The challenge is to balance the trade-off between economic benefit and protection. Sustainable tourism aims to give local communities a real boost while preserving unspoilt places. For travellers, too, there is a role: travelling in the off-season, choosing locally owned businesses and learning to dress modestly at religious sites can reduce the impact of a visit. Tourism has drawbacks, but managed well, it can still be a force for good.
